title: Substitution and Changing the Limits
quickIdea: If the integrand contains a function together with its derivative, substitute that inner function; in a definite integral change the two limits as well and never substitute back.
remember: The pattern to look for is f(g(x)) g'(x): set u = g(x), so du = g'(x) dx, and the integral becomes the integral of f(u) du.
In a definite integral the limits travel with the substitution: x = a gives u = g(a), x = b gives u = g(b). The answer then needs no back-substitution.
If du is off by a constant, adjust the constant - the OpenStax section's example needs du/2 because du = 2z dz while the integrand carries z dz.
Two standard forms cover many GATE integrands: the integral of f'(x)/f(x) is ln|f(x)|, and the integral of f(x) f'(x) is f(x)^2/2.
When the substitution is x = something in t, the derivative dx/dt may be negative, which reverses the limits and adds a sign - that is where most lost marks in 2015 Set 1 Q.44 come from.
Differentiate your chosen u and check the integrand really contains du; if it does not, the substitution is wrong, not the algebra.

example.prompt: Evaluate the integral from 1/pi to 2/pi of cos(1/x)/x^2 dx.
example.work: Take u = 1/x, so du = -dx/x^2, that is dx/x^2 = -du. The limits move: x = 1/pi gives u = pi, and x = 2/pi gives u = pi/2. The integral becomes minus the integral of cos u from pi to pi/2, which equals the integral of cos u from pi/2 to pi. An antiderivative is sin u, so the value is sin(pi) - sin(pi/2) = 0 - 1 = -1.

gateAngle: Two previous-year questions sit on this card. GATE CSE 2015 Set 1 Q.44 is the reciprocal substitution with a sign trap and the answer -1; GATE CSE 2009 Q.25 rewrites (1 - tan x)/(1 + tan x) as a logarithmic derivative and gets (1/2) ln 2. In both, the marks are lost by not changing the limits or by losing the minus sign.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2015 Set 1 Q.44: compute the integral from 1/pi to 2/pi of cos(1/x)/x^2 dx.
variations.why: u = 1/x turns dx/x^2 into -du and moves the limits from (1/pi, 2/pi) to (pi, pi/2). Flipping the limits to remove the minus sign gives the integral of cos u from pi/2 to pi, which is sin(pi) - sin(pi/2) = -1. Forgetting to flip the limits gives +1, the common wrong answer.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2009 Q.25: the integral from 0 to pi/4 of (1 - tan x)/(1 + tan x) dx equals (A) 0 (B) 1 (C) ln 2 (D) (1/2) ln 2.
variations.why: Writing tan x = sin x / cos x makes the integrand (cos x - sin x)/(cos x + sin x), which is exactly the derivative of ln(cos x + sin x) divided by itself. With u = cos x + sin x the limits become 1 and sqrt(2), so the value is ln(sqrt(2)) = (1/2) ln 2 = 0.3466.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is it wrong to substitute u = sin x in the integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin^8 x cos x dx and then keep the limits 0 and pi/2?
variations.answer: Because the limits belong to x, and after substituting they must be rewritten in u: 0 and 1.
variations.why: The correct computation gives the integral of u^8 from 0 to 1, which is 1/9. Keeping the old limits would mean the integral of u^8 from 0 to pi/2, which is (pi/2)^9/9 = 6.46899 instead of 0.1111 - a wildly different number, which is why the limits must travel with the substitution.

trap.what: Changing the integrand but not the limits, or losing the minus sign that comes from du = -dx/x^2.
trap.why: The two limits are values of x, not of u. Once the variable changes, they must change too; and when the substitution is decreasing, the derivative is negative and the limits swap.
trap.counterexample: Substituting u = 1/x in the integral from 1/pi to 2/pi without touching the limits would ask for the integral of cos u from 1/pi to 2/pi, which is sin(2/pi) - sin(1/pi) = 0.5944 - 0.3090 = 0.2854, not -1.

check.question: Evaluate the integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin^8 x cos x dx.
check.explanation: With u = sin x and du = cos x dx the limits become 0 and 1, so the integral is the integral of u^8 from 0 to 1 = 1/9 = 0.1111. The lecture example this is taken from states the same answer.
